## Selling a coffee at the chair without a second till
Source: https://salonforge.com/blog/coffee-at-the-chair-second-till/
Published: 2026-08-19  ·  Updated: 2026-08-19

Plenty of salons have moved past the paper cup of water and the biscuit tin. There's a machine, a proper cup, sometimes a small list — a flat white, a glass of something on a Friday. It's a nice touch, and clients notice it. What most salons haven't moved past is how that drink gets recorded, which is usually: it doesn't, not on the till that everything else goes through.

## Why does a drink kept off the main till matter?

Because the client's bill for that visit stops being the whole story of what happened in the chair. The till shows the cut, the colour, maybe a retail bottle at the end — a clean, correct total for everything that was rung through it. The coffee poured twenty minutes into the appointment was never rung anywhere, so it isn't in that total, even though it was every bit as real a cost and every bit as real a moment of the visit.

That's not a client-facing problem most of the time — nobody's overcharged, nobody complains. It's an owner-facing problem. The bill you can pull up for any client on any day quietly under-describes what you actually gave them, and the till report at the end of the week under-describes what actually left the bar.

## What gets forgotten at the point of pouring?

The drink itself, almost every time — not out of carelessness, but because pouring a coffee doesn't feel like a sale. Ringing up a cut feels like a transaction: it's the reason the client is there, it happens at a desk, near a card machine, at a moment built for it. Pouring a coffee happens mid-appointment, at a machine that's nowhere near the till, done by whoever's hands are free, as a small kindness rather than a line item. Nothing about the moment says "now go and log this."

That's true whether the drink is meant to be charged for or given free. A stylist topping up a client's glass isn't thinking about stock. A receptionist making a coffee between two phone calls isn't thinking about the till. The pour and the record are two separate acts, in two separate places, and only one of them ever happens without being asked to.

The same gap shows up on the shelf behind the bar. Beans, milk, syrup, wine, tonic — all of it depletes across a week exactly the way any product does, and none of it explains itself. Whoever orders more coffee eventually notices the tin's lighter than it should be. What they can't tell you, from a shelf count alone, is which afternoon it went, or whether it went to clients at all.

> A drink that isn't on the bill isn't free — it's just unrecorded. Those are two very different things once you're trying to work out what a Friday actually cost you.

## What's the real difference between a separate till and one bill?

A separate float, notebook or honesty jar for drinks means the record for one visit lives in two places that never check each other.

| | Drinks on a separate till or notebook | Drinks on the client's bill |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What the client's bill shows | Services and retail only — the drink is missing | The whole visit, in one total |
| What the stock count is measured against | A shelf count, checked back to nothing in particular | The actual pour, at the moment it happened |
| Who has to remember to log it | Whoever's free, if they think of it | Nobody — logging the drink and pouring it are the same tap |
| What a Friday night bar tally actually tells you | That some drinks went somewhere | Exactly what was poured, to whom, and what it cost |

Neither side of that table is about honesty. It's about which one produces a number anybody can act on afterwards, and which one just produces a vague sense that the bar "probably breaks even."

## What changes when it lands on the same bill?

The drink stops being a side note and becomes part of the same record as everything else about that visit. It's added to the client's bill at the point it's poured — the same tap that puts it there also takes it off stock, to the ingredient, so nobody has to walk to a till or write anything down separately. That's the shift the [Bar](/bar/) feature in SalonForge is built around: one client record, one till, one stock count, with the drink simply added to it rather than tracked apart from it.

Practically, that means three things line up instead of drifting apart on their own. The client's bill finally shows the full visit — cut, colour, coffee — rather than a partial one. The stock count behind the bar is checked against real pours rather than a shelf guess. And the owner can finally answer the question a separate till never could: does the bar pay for itself, or is it a nice touch that quietly costs more than anyone realised.

## Does the drink need to be charged for this to matter?

No. Plenty of salons decide a coffee is hospitality, not a sale, and never put a price against it — that's a legitimate choice, not a mistake to fix. What still matters is that a zero-price drink gets logged exactly like a paid one, at the same moment, against the same client. The point was never the price. It was always the record. A salon that gives drinks away for free but logs every one of them knows precisely what its hospitality costs across a month. A salon that charges for drinks but only sometimes rings them knows almost nothing, despite technically charging more.

## Start with one till

You don't need to overhaul the bar to see the gap. For one week, try writing down, honestly, every drink that gets poured and never rung anywhere — including the free ones nobody thought to note. Most owners are surprised less by the value of it, which is usually modest, and more by how completely it had been invisible until someone actually looked. That's the whole case for one bill instead of two systems that only half talk to each other: not the size of the number, but the fact that, until now, there wasn't one.

## Reception overwhelmed on a Saturday? What's actually breaking
Source: https://salonforge.com/blog/reception-overwhelmed-saturday/
Published: 2026-08-17  ·  Updated: 2026-08-17

Ask a salon owner what breaks at reception on a Saturday and the answer usually comes out as one sentence: "we just can't keep up." That sentence hides two entirely different problems, and they need entirely different fixes.

One is a staffing problem — genuinely not enough people for the amount of work in the building. The other is a system problem — enough people, but the phone, the till and the walk-in door are all asking the same pair of hands for something at the same moment. Treat the second one like the first and you hire a person into a job that was never short of people, it was short of hands that weren't already doing something else.

## What actually happens on an overwhelmed Saturday

It's rarely one dramatic failure. It's a string of small collisions, each lasting seconds, that add up across a day.

A client is mid-payment at the till when the phone starts ringing. A walk-in asks a question at the desk while reception is already on a call rebooking someone else. Two clients arrive to check in within a minute of each other and only one person is free to greet either. None of these, on their own, look like a crisis. Stacked from nine until closing, they're what "overwhelmed" actually means on the floor.

## Is it staffing, or is it the system?

Ask this of each collision: would a second pair of hands, doing nothing else all day but standing by for this exact moment, actually fix it? If yes, it's staffing. If the second person would be idle for most of the day and only useful in that one collision, it's the system asking one role to do two jobs at once.

| What it looks like | Genuinely a staffing gap | Actually a system problem |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Phone rings while someone's mid-payment at the till | No — a second till wouldn't be busy the rest of the day, only at that moment | Yes — the payment and the call are both asking for the one person free right then |
| Nobody's on the desk because reception is on a break with no cover | Yes — that's a genuine gap in the rota | – |
| A regular calls to rebook and reception has to check three places for a free slot | No | Yes — that's a diary that isn't in front of whoever answers |
| The desk is rammed with people from open to close, every day, not just Saturday | Yes — that's headcount, not a fixable collision | – |
| A walk-in's question interrupts a call that was about to book a slot | No | Yes — two people needed the same one at once |

The pattern in the "system problem" rows is the same every time: the task itself doesn't need more staff, it needs to not be waiting on the one person who's already doing something else.

> A phone ringing while the till is mid-payment is not proof you need a faster receptionist. It's proof one person is being asked to be in two places at once.

## Why switching between the phone and the till costs more than it looks

It costs more than the seconds it takes to glance at the screen and decide whether to answer. Research on workplace interruptions has found that attention does not snap back cleanly once it's been pulled away — a widely cited study from the University of California, Irvine put the average time to fully regain focus after an interruption at around 23 minutes, see [Duke Today's summary of the research](https://today.duke.edu/2021/11/3-ways-bounce-back-after-work-interruption). That study was done on office workers switching between screens, not a salon front desk switching between a card machine and a ringing phone, so the number itself won't transfer directly. What does transfer is the underlying point: a "quick" interruption is never actually quick once you count the run-up to get back to full speed on the first task. On a Saturday, reception rarely gets that run-up before the next thing lands.

It's the same pattern in the salons we work inside, from London to Saudi Arabia — the specific mix of collisions differs by salon, but the split between "not enough people" and "one person doing two jobs at once" doesn't.

## Which parts are genuinely about headcount

Some Saturday strain is real understaffing, and it's worth naming plainly so it doesn't get lost under the system talk.

If there is truly nobody free anywhere in the building — no float for a lunch break, a column booked back to back with zero buffer, a queue that's still there an hour after opening regardless of what the phone is doing — that's a rota problem. More people, or a better-shaped rota, is the honest fix. No amount of moving tasks around removes work that genuinely needs more hands to do it.

## What changes when you fix the right one

If it's staffing, the fix is a person: cover for the break that currently has none, or a second body on the desk for the three worst hours of the week. If it's the system, the fix is removing a task from the collision entirely rather than sharing it — the phone gets answered by something that isn't also holding a card machine, so it stops competing with the payment in the first place. Reception still runs the floor either way. What changes is how often they're asked to be two places at once.

## Where to start

Before spending on either fix, watch what actually collides. For a few Saturdays, note what reception was doing each time the phone rang — not just how many calls came in, but what they were already in the middle of. The [missed-call calculator](/tools/missed-call-calculator/) is a quick way to put a shape on how many of those calls are being lost altogether, which is often the fastest way to see whether the problem is bodies or collisions.

Most owners already know which one it feels like. The point of watching first is making sure the feeling matches what's actually happening at the desk.

## Why hairdressers really leave (and what actually keeps them)
Source: https://salonforge.com/blog/why-stylists-really-leave/
Published: 2026-08-14  ·  Updated: 2026-08-14

A stylist hands in their notice and gives a reason: better money down the road, a shorter commute, a friend's salon with a chair going. It's rarely a lie. It's also rarely the whole story. Ask most owners a week later and they'll admit they saw it coming for months — someone who'd gone a bit quiet, who'd stopped asking about training, who'd never quite got a straight answer about what came next.

Pay is easy to blame, on both sides. It's the reason that fits in one sentence on the way out the door. What's usually sitting underneath it is harder to say out loud, which is exactly why it doesn't get talked about until the notice is already on the desk.

## Is pay really why hairdressers leave?

Rarely on its own. A stylist who leaves for more money is usually worth more money, and the offer is real — but pay alone doesn't explain why this stylist, at this salon, right now. Two stylists on the same rate, doing broadly the same work, don't hand in their notice at the same time or for the same reasons. Something else is usually doing the deciding, and pay is just the version of it that's easiest to say in a resignation conversation.

If pay were the whole story, a modest rise would reliably keep someone who was wobbling. It doesn't reliably work that way, and most owners who've tried it once already know it.

## Can a stylist see their own numbers?

Usually not until payday, and that gap is where a lot of quiet doubt starts. Most stylists have a rough feeling for how a month is going — a good run of colour clients, a quiet fortnight, more retail than usual. If the only place that feeling gets tested against a real figure is a payslip four weeks later, they've had nothing to check it against in between.

That matters most for the stylists worth keeping. A strong stylist usually has some sense of their own market value — what a similar rota elsewhere might pay — and if the only number they can compare it against is a monthly payslip, they're comparing blind. [Performance](/performance/) puts a stylist's own takings, commission and rebooking rate in front of them as the month happens, not only once it's over, so whatever number they're weighing against an offer from down the road is the real one, not a guess carried over from last time.

## What column management actually does to trust

It decides, most days, who feels like the salon's first choice and who feels like the fallback — often without anyone meaning to send that message. New clients, walk-ins and cover for someone else's no-show all have to land somewhere, and where they land says something, whether or not it was said out loud.

A junior who keeps getting the walk-ins nobody else wants, and rarely a new client booked in against their own name, is getting a message about where they sit. A senior stylist whose column keeps being padded out to cover someone else's gaps is getting a different message, just as clearly. Neither shows up as a complaint, usually. It shows up as someone a bit less keen about a Tuesday, months before it shows up as a notice.

> The stylists who leave quietest are rarely the ones who were struggling. They're the ones nobody had a proper conversation with, in either direction, for a year.

## Why education keeps coming up when stylists leave

Because it's the clearest signal a stylist has for whether the salon still sees a future in them. A stylist who hasn't learned a new technique or been on a course in a year or two starts asking a fairly reasonable question: is the salon still investing in me, or am I just filling a slot on the rota? Nobody frames it that starkly to themselves. It shows up smaller — noticing a colleague went on a course and they weren't asked, or that the last training day was a while back and nobody's mentioned the next one.

Education is one of the cheaper things a salon can offer next to pay, and one of the first things to slip when the diary's full and there's no obvious hour to spare for it. That trade-off is understandable on a busy week. Repeated over a year, it reads to a stylist as a decision about them, even when it was never meant as one.

## Being told where they stand

Most stylists don't need to hear they're doing brilliantly. They need to hear something, on a schedule, rather than nothing until there's a problem. Feedback that only turns up when something's gone wrong teaches a stylist that silence means there's nothing to worry about — right up until the day it doesn't.

A short conversation a few times a year, covering what's working, what isn't, and what would move someone up or move their pay on, does something a payslip and an occasional word in passing can't: it tells a stylist their future in the salon is something the owner actually thinks about, not something being decided by default.

## What actually keeps someone

| What's often said on the way out | What's often underneath it |
| --- | --- |
| "Better money" | No visibility of their own numbers, to know if the current pay was even fair |
| "Needed a change" | An uneven column, felt for months before anyone named it |
| "Time to move on" | No new technique or training in a year or more |
| "It just wasn't working" | Nobody had told them plainly where they stood, in either direction |

None of this is about blaming an owner for not noticing, or a stylist for wanting more. Most salons are run by someone managing a full diary and a full rota at the same time, and most of what's in that table is invisible unless you go looking for it. It isn't about pay mattering less, either — pay matters, and always will. It's that pay is the one thing that's easy to check and easy to talk about, and the rest of the table usually isn't.

## Where to start

With whichever one of the four you can't currently answer for your own team. Does each stylist know roughly how their month is going right now, not just on payday? Has their column been fair over the last few months, not just today? When did they last learn something new? And when did you last tell them, plainly, where they stand?

A salon that can answer all four for every chair is rare. Most can answer two. The gap between two and four is usually cheaper to close than a pay rise — and it's the one more likely to be the reason someone stays through a wobble instead of quietly updating their CV.

---

## From application to first shift: a hiring plan for a small salon
Source: https://salonforge.com/blog/hiring-plan-first-shift/
Published: 2026-08-12  ·  Updated: 2026-08-12

There is no single hard part of hiring a stylist. There are six small ones, each easy enough to do between a blow-dry and a colour consultation: write the advert, reply to the application, make the call, run the trade test, send the offer, get the first day right. Almost every hiring process that drags on for months hasn't failed at any one of those steps - it has stalled at one of them, usually because it was waiting for a desk and a spare hour that a working salon rarely has.

This is the sequence laid out in order, with what "good" looks like at each stage, and more detail on the step most owners get wrong without realising it: the trade test.

## What the whole sequence looks like

Six steps, and each one has its own short deadline that has nothing to do with how busy the salon is that week.

| Step | What good looks like | How long it should take |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Advert | The real room, the rota pattern and the pay structure, stated plainly | Reviewed daily, however long it runs |
| First reply | A message sent the same day it lands, even a short one | Same day |
| Phone call | Three questions in order: can they start, what they do, why this salon | About ten minutes |
| Trade test | Real or model client, alongside a working stylist, on an ordinary-Tuesday brief | 60-90 minutes |
| Offer | Days, pay, notice period and start date, confirmed in writing | Within a day of the trade test |
| First day | Chair ready, rota entry made, someone assigned to show them round | Arranged before they arrive |

None of this is complicated on its own. What breaks it is one step sitting untouched for a week, because the only time anyone had to think about hiring was a Sunday evening that never quite arrived.

## The advert and the first reply: both move within a day

The advert has one job: get an application from someone who could actually do the work on offer, so say plainly what the work is. Use a photo of the real room, not a stock image; the actual rota pattern, not "flexible hours"; and the pay structure, not a range so wide it tells a stylist nothing about what they'd actually take home. A vague advert doesn't attract fewer people - it attracts the wrong ones, who find out at the phone call that the job was never what they thought it was.

The reply matters more than the advert did. Whoever applied is almost certainly applying elsewhere too, and the salon that answers first is the one still in the running by the time a trade test gets booked. A reply sent from a phone at the till - "got this, will call you Thursday" - beats a well-written message sent four days later. Answer it the day it lands, not the day there's finally time to write something good.

## What should the phone call actually cover?

Three things, in this order: can they actually start, what they actually do, and why this salon rather than any salon with a chair going. Notice period and the days on offer come first, because there's no point discussing technique with someone who can't work your rota. What they specialise in, and how they describe their own clients, comes second - a vague answer here is usually a sign of a vague stylist. Why this salon comes last, because someone who mentions something specific about the place is a different prospect from someone working down a list of open tabs. Ten minutes is enough. If all three land, book the trade test before you hang up.

## What does a good trade test actually look like?

A short, real session - not a performance, and not your hardest technical case. Sixty to ninety minutes, on a real or model client, alongside one of your own stylists, given the kind of brief they'd actually get on an ordinary Tuesday. If you can pay them for the time, do - it's work, even if it's short, and a paid trial tells a candidate you take the process as seriously as you're asking them to.

What you're watching for is mostly things you can see rather than things they say. Do they check in with the client partway through, or carry on regardless of what was actually asked for? Does their station stay usable, or does it spread across the whole back bar? Do they clean up without being asked? And, worth more than any of it, what does the rest of the team say about them once they've gone, unprompted - that reaction tends to be a better predictor than anything said in the call.

> A trade test isn't there to catch someone out. It's there to answer one question honestly: could this person be in front of my clients tomorrow?

Debrief with whoever they worked alongside the same day, while it's still fresh. A verdict formed a week later, from memory, isn't much better than no trade test at all.

## The offer: what needs to be pinned down before anyone gives notice

Four things, in writing, within a day of the trade test: days and hours, how the pay actually works, the notice period, and a start date. This is where good intentions turn into a candidate who quietly stops replying - not because the money was wrong, but because nothing was confirmed while a clearer offer came in from somewhere else. Put the same four things in writing every time, whether the role is employed, commission or chair rental, so nobody is negotiating from memory a week later.

## The first day: what makes it feel planned, not lucky

A chair that's actually ready, a name on the rota, and someone whose job it is to show them round - all decided before the trade test is even finished, not worked out at the front desk while they're stood there in their coat. Getting someone from an application to standing at a chair on a real first shift is the exact span SalonForge's [People](/people/) product is built to cover, so the trade test notes and the rota entry are the same record rather than a note on a phone that has to be typed in from memory later.

None of the six steps here need a recruitment background or a quiet afternoon. They need doing on the day they come up, in the gaps between clients, in the order above. That's usually the whole difference between a chair that fills in a fortnight and one that's been advertised since spring.

---

## Why can't I find hairdressers? Recruiting stylists in 2026
Source: https://salonforge.com/blog/recruiting-stylists-shortage/
Published: 2026-08-10  ·  Updated: 2026-08-10

If the chair has been sitting in your advert since spring and the applications are either thin or wrong for the room, it is worth saying plainly: it isn't just you, and it probably isn't the advert either. Hairdressing is short of people, and it has been getting shorter for a while.

That doesn't make the empty chair any less expensive. It does change what's worth fixing. If the problem were your wording, a better headline would solve it. It won't, because the wording was never really the constraint.

## Is there actually a shortage of hairdressers?

Yes, and it shows up in the numbers behind apprenticeships and vacancies, not just in how the chair-hunt feels.

Apprentice numbers in hairdressing and beauty fell from around 16,000 to 6,000 between 2016 and 2023, according to [research by CBI Economics for the British Hair Consortium](https://feweek.co.uk/hairdressing-apprenticeships-face-extinction-under-labour-tax-rises-says-report/), which forecasts that on current trends the number could fall to zero by 2027. Separately, the NHBF's [Careers at the Cutting Edge report](https://hji.co.uk/how-to-tackle-the-hair-industrys-skills-and-recruitment-crisis) found that 57% of hair and beauty businesses have unfilled vacancies, and more than half of those vacancies take over 16 weeks to fill.

That second figure is the one worth sitting with. Sixteen weeks is not "we'll find someone eventually." It's most of a school term, most of a busy season, most of the runway a struggling column needs before it starts costing you clients as well as chair time.

## Where do stylists actually look for a chair?

Mostly not on a general job board. Word of mouth, social media and other salons are where the search actually happens.

A stylist thinking about moving usually hears about a chair from another stylist first — someone they trained with, someone who used to work down the road, someone in a shared industry Facebook group. After that, they'll look at a salon's own social feed, because it tells them more about the room than a job spec does: who's on the floor, what the work looks like, whether the place feels like somewhere they'd want to be on a Saturday. Local colleges are worth a real relationship rather than an occasional work-experience slot — the good ones you meet at 17 are still good at 22, and by then they're not cheap or easy to find any other way.

A general job listing still has a place. It just isn't where the strongest candidates start looking, because in a genuine shortage the best people aren't scrolling adverts — they're already employed, and moving only for a chair someone told them about directly.

## Why speed of reply beats advert wording

Because a stylist worth having is rarely reading only your advert, and the salon that replies first gets first go at a trial.

They're usually weighing up two or three chairs at once. None of that comparison happens on the strength of the sentence describing the role — it happens on who actually gets back to them, and how quickly. A same-day reply, even a short one confirming you've seen the application and naming a day you'll call, keeps you in that comparison. Silence takes you out of it, and it does that regardless of how good the advert underneath was.

> A stylist choosing between three unanswered adverts and one salon that called back by the end of the day isn't choosing on wording. They're choosing on who called back.

This is also why polishing the advert usually isn't the fix people hope it is. A stronger headline gets you a few more applications into the same slow reply process. It doesn't touch the part that's actually losing you candidates.

## What a chair needs to offer beyond pay

Pay gets the advert read. What keeps someone in the chair, and keeps them applying to begin with, is usually something else.

In a genuine shortage, most chairs on offer are paying something reasonable — a rate on its own rarely separates one advert from another. What does separate them is whether the rest of the offer holds up once someone's actually in the room.

| What gets someone to apply | What keeps them once they're in the chair |
| --- | --- |
| The headline rate | Whether they can see their own numbers, not take a payslip on trust |
| A tidy job description | A rota that doesn't swallow the week without warning |
| A salon they've heard of | Ongoing education, not a one-off induction |
| A photo of a nice interior | Being told plainly where they stand and what moves them up |

None of the right-hand column replaces fair pay. It's what makes the pay worth staying for, once the novelty of a new chair has worn off.

## Why the salons that reply within a day hire best

Not because they're doing anything clever — because they aren't losing candidates to whoever replied first.

Most of what separates a salon that hires well from one that doesn't isn't a better read on talent. It's that the good candidates are still available to be read at all. Reply within a day, structure a short call around whether someone can actually start, what they do, and why this salon specifically, and you're making the same decision a slower process would have reached — while the strongest people are still on the table.

## Start with the reply

If the advert isn't the problem, don't spend another week rewriting it. Spend that time on how fast an application actually gets a reply, because that's the step where candidates are being lost before you ever get to judge their work.

We've written before in more detail about [what that first-day reply and the trade test that follows should actually look like](/blog/screening-stylist-applicants/) — this piece is about getting someone through the door in a market that's short of people to begin with. The shortage isn't going away on its own. Being the salon that replies today, in a market where most don't, is still one of the few advantages entirely within your own control.

---

## Hybrid pay: mixing rent, commission and salary without the maths falling apart
Source: https://salonforge.com/blog/hybrid-pay-rent-commission-salary/
Published: 2026-08-07  ·  Updated: 2026-08-07

Ask a salon owner how they pay their team and the honest answer is rarely one word. It's usually "the two senior colourists are on commission, the juniors are on salary, and the barber at the end rents his own chair" — three different arrangements, running side by side, under one roof.

That's not disorganised. It's what a salon that's grown over several years actually looks like. The trouble starts somewhere else entirely: not in having three models, but in three models each drawing on a different version of what was actually taken that week.

## Why does hybrid pay usually go wrong?

It goes wrong when the takings feeding each pay rule aren't the same figures for every chair. A salon with one employed team and one till has a single number everyone trusts. Add a rented chair with its own card machine, or a junior whose retail gets logged separately "to keep it simple," and you now have several versions of the truth sitting in different corners of the business — a diary total here, a till total there, a notebook for the chair that rents.

Nobody sets out to build it that way. It happens gradually: a new stylist joins on a different deal than everyone else, a rented chair keeps their own float, a locum comes in for a month on a rate nobody's used before. Each change is reasonable on its own. Together, they mean payroll day involves reconciling several different records instead of reading one.

> The problem was never having three pay models. It was having three versions of what actually got taken.

## What has to be true before hybrid pay works?

One set of takings that every pay rule reads from, whatever that chair's arrangement is. It doesn't matter whether a stylist is on salary, commission, or paying rent — the figure of what they actually took that day needs to come from the same place: the till, not a memory, not a side notebook, not an estimate carried over from last month because nobody had time to check.

Once that's true, applying different rules to different chairs stops being complicated. Rent doesn't move with a quiet week; commission does. A salary is fixed regardless of takings; a rented chair's income to the owner is fixed regardless of the stylist's takings. None of that is hard maths. It only gets hard when the number each rule is being applied to isn't reliable in the first place.

| Pay model | What moves with takings | What the owner is owed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Salary | Nothing — fixed pay regardless of the week | The full service price, minus costs |
| Commission | The stylist's take-home | A share of every service, set by the rate |
| Chair rental | Nothing for the owner — rent is fixed | A fixed rent, whatever the chair took |

## Why do written-down rules matter more than clever spreadsheets?

Because a rule that only exists in someone's head gets applied differently under pressure. A commission rate that's "roughly 40%, more for colour, a bit different for retail" sounds fine in conversation and falls apart the moment two stylists compare payslips and the maths doesn't quite match between them. Not because anyone was cutting corners — because nobody wrote the rule down precisely enough for it to be applied the same way twice.

This matters more, not less, once you're mixing models. A salon running one pay structure for everyone can get away with an informal rule staying roughly consistent, because everyone's watching the same thing happen to everyone else. A salon running three structures at once has no such safety net — a junior on salary has no way to sanity-check whether the senior colourist's commission was worked out correctly, so the only thing protecting that number from drifting is whether the rule was actually written down and applied the same way every time.

Written down doesn't have to mean complicated. It means: this rate, on this service type, for this chair, calculated from this number — set once, applied consistently, not re-decided from memory on a Friday afternoon.

## Why does it help for stylists to see the number before payday?

Because a number that only appears once, on payday, gives a stylist nothing to check it against. Whatever their pay model, most stylists have a rough feeling for how their month is going — a good run of colour clients, a quiet fortnight, a big retail week. If the figure that eventually lands on their payslip has never been visible before that moment, there's no way for them to notice a mistake, or trust that there isn't one.

That's true across every model in a hybrid set-up, not just commission. A salaried stylist wants to see their targets and bonus thresholds moving through the month. A chair-rental stylist wants to see, at a glance, that the rent being taken matches the agreement rather than a figure they have to take on trust. Visibility isn't a nice extra bolted onto one pay type — it's what stops payday being the first moment anyone finds out whether the maths held up.

## What does this actually look like on a normal payroll day?

Quiet, mostly. Each chair's takings for the month are already sitting in one place, because that's where the till has been recording them all along — not reconstructed from three different logs the night before payroll is due. The rent rule runs against the rented chairs. The commission rule runs against the commissioned ones. Salaries go out as agreed. Nobody is cross-referencing a paper diary against a spreadsheet against a card machine total to work out who took what.

The interesting work happens earlier in the month, not on payroll day itself — deciding whether a rate is still right, whether a chair should move from commission to rental, whether a junior is ready to come off a training wage. Those are business decisions. They only get to be business decisions, rather than arguments about whose figures are correct, once the underlying takings are something everyone already agrees on. [Performance](/performance/) reads every sale straight from the till so rent, commission and salary are all worked out from the same figures, whatever mix of models a salon is actually running.

## Where to start

Write down, chair by chair, which model applies and what the exact rule is — not roughly, precisely enough that two people would calculate the same payslip from the same week's takings. Most of the maths in hybrid pay was never the hard part. Getting everyone to agree on the number it started from was.

---

## Chair rental vs employed stylists: what UK salon owners are weighing up in 2026
Source: https://salonforge.com/blog/chair-rental-vs-employed-stylists/
Published: 2026-08-05  ·  Updated: 2026-08-05

Ask five salon owners whether to employ their stylists or rent them chairs and you'll get five confident, different answers. That's not because one side is wrong — it's because both models genuinely work, for salons chasing different things. This isn't a debate with a correct answer. It's a set of trade-offs, and the trade you're actually making is usually not the one people argue about loudest.

## What's actually different between the two models?

The stylist's status changes who controls what, more than it changes how much money moves. Under an employed model, the salon sets prices, decides the treatment menu, owns the client list, and pays a wage — plus holiday pay, sick pay and the rest — whether the week is heaving or dead. In return, the salon keeps everything the chair takes.

Under chair rental, the stylist is effectively a small business paying to use your space. They set their own prices, choose their own hours, take their own bookings and usually keep their own client list. In return, you get a fixed rent — or an agreed percentage — that doesn't move much whether their diary is full or half-empty.

| | Employed stylist | Chair rental |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Who sets the price | The salon | The stylist |
| Who owns the client relationship | The salon | Usually the stylist |
| Who carries the risk on a quiet week | The owner — wages still due | The stylist — rent still due |
| Who controls standards and brand | The salon | Limited — a genuine rental can't dictate this |
| What the owner keeps | The full service price, minus costs | A fixed rent or share, however busy the chair is |

## What does each model do to your cash flow?

It decides whether your income moves with the diary or sits apart from it. Employed stylists mean your takings rise and fall with how busy the salon actually is — good on a booked-out Saturday, painful in a quiet January when wages are still due regardless. Chair rental flattens that: the rent comes in whether the stylist's day is full or empty, so your income is steadier, but you no longer see a share of their brilliant week either. You've swapped upside for certainty.

## Who ends up owning the client?

Usually the stylist, under chair rental — and that's the trade owners tend to underestimate most. A stylist who rents a chair typically built, or brought, their own client book, keeps their own contact details, and takes bookings directly. If they leave, in most genuine rental set-ups their clients go with them, because the relationship was always theirs rather than the salon's.

> A chair-rental salon doesn't lose a stylist when someone leaves. It loses a stylist and their diary, on the same day.

Under employment, the salon usually holds the client record instead, so a stylist leaving is a staffing gap rather than a client exodus — though a well-liked stylist can still take some loyalty with them regardless of what the contract says on paper.

## Can you keep the salon's standards the same either way?

Not to the same degree. An employed stylist can be asked to follow the salon's protocols — the retail line they promote, the finish they're trained to deliver, the hours they're expected to keep. A genuine chair-rental stylist is running their own business inside your building, which means you can offer guidance but can't require it without risking the arrangement no longer looking like a rental at all. Salons that care deeply about one consistent standard across every chair tend to lean employed; salons happy to be a collection of independent specialists under one roof tend to lean rental.

## Where does chair rental cross into being an employment relationship?

This is the part worth being careful about, and it isn't a call to make on habit or on what the salon down the road happens to do. HMRC has published dedicated guidance for the hair and beauty sector because the two arrangements get blurred so often in practice — a stylist who "rents" a chair but is told what to charge, which hours to work and which clients to take is, in substance, being treated as an employee, whatever the paperwork says. Getting that wrong has real consequences on both sides: unpaid holiday pay, National Minimum Wage claims, and tax liabilities that land after the fact rather than at the time.

We're not going to tell you where that line sits for your salon — that's a job for an accountant or an employment specialist who can look at your actual agreement and how it plays out day to day, not a blog post. [GOV.UK's guidance for hair and beauty](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/check-employment-status-if-you-work-in-hair-and-beauty) is a reasonable place to start before you set an arrangement up, and worth revisiting if an existing one has drifted from what's written down.

Self-employment is already the default across the sector rather than the exception. Across hairdressing and barbering, [58% of the workforce is self-employed](https://www.nhbf.co.uk/advice-and-resources/hair-and-beauty-industry-statistics/), according to NHBF's industry figures — chair and room renters among them, alongside mobile and home-based stylists. The question for most owners isn't really whether to allow it. It's how much of the salon to run that way, and how carefully the arrangement is set up.

## Which model actually suits your salon?

It depends on what you're trying to protect — consistency or flexibility. A salon built around a strong single brand, a tight retail push and a house style tends to do better employed, because that's the model that actually lets you enforce those things. A salon built around a handful of established names who each bring their own following — a senior colourist, a specialist barber — often does better letting them rent, because trying to fold an established independent operator into a uniform structure usually just causes friction. Most salons that have been trading a while end up running some version of both, which is its own kind of complicated and a subject for another day.

## What stays true whichever model you choose?

You still need one clear number for what each chair actually took, whoever it belongs to. A mix of employed and rented chairs means rent, commission and wages are being worked out differently for different people under the same roof, and that's exactly the kind of thing that goes wrong quietly on a spreadsheet — a rent payment missed, a commission calculated on the wrong week, a stylist who can't see their own numbers and has to take the salon's word for it. Whichever model, or mix, you run, [Performance](/performance/) reads every sale straight from the till, so rent, commission and take-home are worked out from what actually happened at the chair, not from a tally someone reconstructs at the end of the month.

## Where to start

Write down, honestly, what you're trying to protect — brand consistency, cash flow certainty, or the freedom to bring in a specialist without putting them on payroll. That answer points you toward a model faster than any comparison table can, this one included. Then get the paperwork checked by someone qualified before you rely on it.

---

## Back bar vs retail: keeping salon stock numbers honest
Source: https://salonforge.com/blog/back-bar-vs-retail-stock/
Published: 2026-08-03  ·  Updated: 2026-08-03

Ask a salon owner what retail took last month and they'll have it from the till in seconds. Ask what went out the back door in services — the colour, the conditioner, the wax scooped out during a blow-dry — and the answer gets vaguer fast, because none of it was ever rung anywhere. It was just used.

That's where most stock confusion starts: two different kinds of product, counted the same way, or not really counted at all. Split the counting properly and most of the confusion goes with it.

## What's the difference between back bar and retail stock?

Back bar is product used on a client during a service; retail is product sold for a client to take home. The same bottle can be either, depending on which shelf it leaves from — poured into a jug at the basin, it's back bar; boxed up at the till, it's retail. The product itself doesn't decide which one it is. What happens to it does.

That's why the two can't be counted the same way. Back bar use is tied to an appointment, with no separate transaction to catch it. Retail use is tied to a sale, and should be rung at the till with a price and a receipt, the same as stock in any other shop.

## Why one number covering both tells you nothing

A single combined stock figure blends two problems that have nothing in common, which is exactly why nobody can act on it.

| Question | One combined number | Back bar and retail counted apart |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Is a stylist overusing product in services? | Invisible, lost in the total | Visible, per stylist, per week |
| Is retail walking out unpaid or under-rung? | Invisible, lost in the total | Visible against till receipts |
| Which shelf needs attention first? | Unanswerable | Whichever count is furthest out |

> A number that covers two different shelves can only ever tell you that something's wrong somewhere. It can't tell you where to look next.

## Counting the back bar

Tie back bar counts to what the diary says was used, not to what's physically left on the shelf.

Back bar has no till transaction of its own, so a shelf count on its own only proves the total is down — it can't say why. The workable fix is recording use at the moment it happens: a stylist logs what went on a head against that appointment, or the amount is weighed, so the figure written down and the amount actually used are the same act rather than two steps that can quietly drift apart over a month.

In practice that means counting the high-value back bar lines — colour, bond builders, the treatment used on nearly every head — weekly, against what that week's appointments say should have gone out. A gap found weekly is small enough to trace back to an actual day. A gap found once a year is just a number with no story attached.

## Counting retail

Tie retail counts to till sales every week, not to a single check against the original delivery note months later.

Retail should behave like stock in any shop: a barcode, a price, a receipt. The count that matters is till sales against physical stock — how many left the shelf against how many were rung as sold. When the two don't match, the usual explanations are mundane rather than dramatic: something rung under the wrong code, a staff purchase that was never logged, a bottle moved onto the back bar shelf by someone in a hurry between clients. Things sold or poured at the chair — a coffee, a glass of something — belong in the same weekly reconciliation, which is the whole idea behind how the [Bar](/bar/) in SalonForge logs a drink against the client and the stock the moment it's poured, rather than leaving it for someone to remember at the end of the week.

## When the two get blurred

Back bar and retail blur every time a product crosses from one shelf to the other without anyone writing it down.

A retail sachet handed to a client having a bad day with their colour is a kind gesture and a back bar use — but if it's never logged, it reads as a retail loss with no service to explain it. A back bar bottle running low at the basin gets topped up from a retail bottle pulled off the shelf because nobody reordered in time — retail goes down, back bar looks fine, and neither number reflects what actually happened.

None of this is theft or carelessness. It's what happens by default when moving a bottle from one shelf to the other takes no more effort than moving it, and writing it down takes a spare minute nobody has on a Saturday.

## A rhythm that holds up on a Saturday

Little and often, split by shelf, beats one large count that mixes both.

| When | Back bar | Retail |
| --- | --- | --- |
| At delivery | Check against the delivery note before it's shelved | Check in against the delivery note before it's priced up |
| Weekly | Count high-value lines against what the diary says was used | Reconcile against till sales for the week |
| Monthly | Spot-check the rest of the range | Full shelf count against the till report |

Splitting the count isn't extra work — it's the same work sorted into the right pile. A back bar gap points you at the diary and the week it opened up. A retail gap points you at the till and the shelf it came from. Keep them apart from the start, and the number you end up with is one you can actually do something about.

---

## How to reduce no-shows in a UK salon without annoying your clients
Source: https://salonforge.com/blog/salon-no-shows-deposits-reminders/
Published: 2026-07-31  ·  Updated: 2026-07-31

A no-show costs a salon in a very particular way: the chair sits empty at exactly the time it was reserved, usually with too little notice to fill it with anyone else. Every owner ends up with their own way of handling it — a line in the booking confirmation, a deposit taken up front, a text sent the night before. None of it gets a salon to zero, and it isn't supposed to. The realistic aim is fewer no-shows, without turning every booking into a negotiation.

## What's the difference between a no-show and a late cancellation?

A no-show is a client who simply doesn't turn up, with no warning at all. A late cancellation is a client who does let you know — just not with enough notice for you to fill the slot. Both leave you with an empty chair at the time it was booked, so the cost to the till is nearly identical. But they aren't the same thing to the client sitting across from you at their next visit, and a policy that charges both at the same rate tends to feel wrong to the person who at least tried to tell you.

Most workable policies draw a line: cancel with more notice than the cut-off (say, 24 or 48 hours) and nothing is charged; cancel inside it, or don't show at all, and the same charge applies to both. That's not because the two are equally bad — it's because once you're inside the cut-off, the chair is equally lost either way.

## Do deposits actually stop no-shows?

Broadly, yes. Asking someone to put money down on a booking makes them more likely to keep it — that's not a controversial claim, it's just what a deposit is for. The part that gets left out of most advice on this is what it costs you to take one.

A deposit is friction at the point of booking, and some clients who would have shown up perfectly reliably will book somewhere else rather than pay one — particularly a first-time client who has no history with you yet and no particular reason to trust the process. You don't get to see those lost bookings; you only see the no-shows you prevented. That's what makes this hard to weigh up from the inside.

> A deposit doesn't remove the choice between a full diary and a protected one. It just moves that choice earlier — to the point of booking, instead of the point where the chair is empty.

There's no single right answer here, and anyone who tells you there is hasn't run a front desk. A busy colour specialist with a six-week waiting list and a high no-show rate is weighing this up very differently from a quiet salon trying to build a client base. Reasonable owners land in different places — deposits on everyone, deposits on new clients only, deposits on long or expensive services only, or no deposits and a harder line on repeat offenders instead. What matters is picking on purpose, rather than copying whatever the salon down the road does.

## Why does reminder timing matter more than what the reminder says?

Because a reminder can only stop a no-show if it arrives while the client can still do something about it — cancel properly, or move the appointment — and that's almost entirely a question of when it lands, not how it's worded.

A message that arrives an hour before the appointment reads as a heads-up, not a chance to act. If the client had already forgotten, an hour isn't enough time to do anything except turn up late or not at all — it confirms attendance for people who were coming anyway and does almost nothing for the ones who weren't. A reminder sent with real notice — the evening before, or a few days out — gives a client who's double-booked themselves, or whose plans changed, an actual window to tell you and free the slot for someone else.

| When the reminder lands | What it can actually catch |
| --- | --- |
| An hour or two before | Confirms clients who were already coming; too late for anyone else to act |
| The evening before | A genuine window to cancel or move — enough notice to still fill the slot |
| Several days before | Long enough to offer the slot to someone on a waiting list if it's freed up |

A review of studies on hospital appointment reminders — a much bigger and better-researched version of the same problem — found that patients who got a reminder were, on average, about 11% more likely to attend than those who got none, and that sending two reminders spaced apart (roughly a week out, then a few days out) worked better than one message close to the appointment. See [the review on jhmhp.amegroups.org](https://jhmhp.amegroups.org/article/view/10215/html). Hospital bookings aren't salon bookings, but the underlying logic transfers: a reminder that arrives too late to act on can only confirm, never rescue.

## What does a policy clients actually accept look like?

One they hear about before they need it, that's applied the same way regardless of who's on the front desk that day, and that charges for what was actually lost rather than the full service price on principle. A client who finds out about a no-show fee for the first time when they're being charged for it has a fair complaint, even if the policy itself is reasonable — the problem is the surprise, not the fee.

Consistency is the part that quietly breaks down in practice. A deposit taken over the phone that never makes it onto the client's record at the desk is a policy that only exists for whoever happened to answer that call. It's easier to hold together when the deposit, the reminder and the booking itself sit against the same record rather than three separate ones a stylist has to cross-check by memory on a Saturday — which is part of what [Daviana](/daviana/) is built to hold together.

## Where to start

Split your own no-show numbers into the two categories from the first section — true no-shows and late cancellations — before you touch pricing or wording. That split alone usually tells you more than a policy change would: a salon with mostly late cancellations has a reminder-timing problem, and a salon with genuine no-shows has a deposit or a repeat-client problem. They don't get fixed by the same lever, and it's worth knowing which one you actually have before you pick one.

---

## Double-booked again? Why salon diaries clash and how to stop it
Source: https://salonforge.com/blog/salon-diary-double-booking/
Published: 2026-07-29  ·  Updated: 2026-07-29

## Why do diaries clash in the first place?

Not because anyone was careless. A double-booking almost always means two systems each held their own version of the diary, and neither one knew what the other had just done.

Picture a normal Saturday morning. A client books a colour appointment online for 2pm. Ten minutes later, someone else rings the desk and asks for the same slot, and whoever answers checks the book — the paper one, or a screen that hasn't caught up with the online page yet — and it still shows 2pm as free. Both clients get a yes. One of them turns up to a chair that's already taken.

Nobody did anything wrong. The person on the phone gave an honest answer, from the version of the diary in front of them. It just wasn't the same version the online page had already changed.

## Where the separate versions actually come from

Most salons run at least three: the online booking page, the phone, and the front desk book — paper, a spreadsheet, or a screen that isn't quite the one clients see. Walk-ins add a fourth, written down after the fact rather than checked against anything first.

Each one is perfectly usable on its own. The trouble starts when a booking made in one of them doesn't reach the others straight away — and "straight away" is the hard part, because it means every one of those places has to be looking at the same diary at the same moment, not a copy of it from five minutes ago.

## What actually happens in the gap

The clash doesn't happen at the moment of booking. It happens in the space between one system taking a slot and the others finding out it's gone.

| Where the booking is made | What it's checking against | How the clash opens up |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Online booking page | Whatever the diary showed the last time it loaded | A slot taken seconds ago by phone may not show as gone yet |
| Phone / front desk | The paper book, or a screen at the desk | Doesn't know what was booked online minutes earlier |
| Walk-in, written down after | Nothing, until someone copies it across later | Sits outside the diary entirely until someone remembers |

That middle column is the whole problem. Every one of those places is telling the truth about what it can see. None of them can see the others.

> A double-booking isn't two people lying about the same slot. It's two systems each telling the truth, from a version of the diary that's already gone stale.

## Does having more ways to book make this worse?

No — and it's worth saying plainly, because the instinct is often to close down a channel rather than fix the gap. A client being able to book online, by phone or at the desk isn't the risk. The risk is how many separate places that booking can land once it's made.

A salon that only ever took bookings at the desk, in one paper book, could never double-book — there was only ever one version of the diary, and it was sitting right there. The moment a second way to book appears, whether that's an online page, a second desk, or a phone line, the diary either stays one diary that all of them read and write to, or it splits into as many versions as there are ways in. Splitting is what causes the clash, not the number of doors.

Rebooking makes the same point from the other direction. A client who cancels at the desk and a client who reschedules online at the same moment are both changing the same diary — and if the desk and the online page aren't looking at each other, the slot that just opened up can be handed to two different people within minutes of each other. The clash isn't new business colliding with new business. It's just as often a cancellation colliding with someone else's reschedule.

## What one diary actually changes

When the online page, the phone and the front desk are all reading and writing the same diary, the gap in that table above stops existing — not because anyone checks faster, but because there's nothing left to catch up on. A slot taken by phone at 11:04 is gone for the online page at 11:04, because it's the same booking, seen from a different screen. We've written before about [what that looks like when the phone itself is doing the booking](/blog/ai-receptionist-real-diary/): the reason two callers can't be told the same slot is free isn't clever checking, it's that there was only ever one diary to check against.

Nothing changes about how clients book. They still ring, still book online, still walk in. What stops is the front desk finding out about a clash after the fact — from an apologetic phone call, or a client standing at the counter expecting a chair that's already occupied.

## Where to start if this is already happening to you

Count the places a booking can land before it reaches the diary the front desk actually works from. If the honest answer is more than one — online page, phone notes, a paper book, a second screen — that count is your clash risk, not how many clients you're seeing.

You don't need to change how clients reach you to fix it. You need every one of those doors opening onto the same diary, so a slot taken through any of them is gone for all of them, at the same moment, without anyone having to notice.

---

## Screening stylist applicants without spending a week reading CVs
Source: https://salonforge.com/blog/screening-stylist-applicants/
Published: 2026-07-24  ·  Updated: 2026-07-24

Most salon owners hire between clients. An application lands while you are half-way through a colour, or at the till at close, and it goes into a mental pile marked "later." Later is usually Sunday night. By Sunday night, the days have already slipped by, and the stylist you most wanted to see has already had a trial somewhere that replied earlier in the week.

This is not a hiring-skill problem. It is a timing problem wearing a hiring-skill costume. Fix the timing and the rest gets much easier.

## Why the CV is the wrong thing to screen on

A CV tells you a stylist's work history. It does not tell you whether they can do the job in your salon.

Years of experience, salon names, a list of brands they have trained on — none of it tells you how someone behaves in front of a client who has brought in a phone photo of someone else's hair and expects to walk out looking like it. It does not tell you whether they rebook, whether they upsell without being pushy, whether they can keep a chair moving on a Saturday without rushing anyone. Those are the things that actually decide whether a hire works out, and none of them are on the page.

| What the CV tells you | What it doesn't tell you |
| --- | --- |
| Where they've worked and for how long | Whether they kept clients, or churned through them |
| Brands and courses they've trained on | Whether they can actually execute a technique start to finish, on time |
| Job titles (senior stylist, colour specialist) | How they talk to a nervous client, or one who won't stop talking |
| Employment gaps | Whether the gap was a baby, a bad salon, or something worth asking about gently |
| A tidy, well-formatted document | Whether they can keep a chair moving without rushing the client |
| That they can list "team player" | Whether the rest of the team will actually want to work beside them |

None of this means the CV is useless. It tells you enough to decide whether to pick up the phone. It just should not be the thing you spend a week reading, because the answers you actually need are not written down anywhere on it.

> A CV tells you where someone has been. It never tells you what they do when a client's hair does not match the photo.

## Why a trade test beats an interview

A trade test beats an interview because it shows you the work instead of a description of the work.

An interview is a conversation about hairdressing. A trade test is hairdressing. Sit a candidate down with a model or a willing friend, next to one of your own stylists, and give them a real or close-to-real brief — nothing elaborate, just something they would actually be asked to do on a normal Tuesday. In a short session you learn more than a long interview would give you:

- **Consultation.** Do they ask what the client actually wants, or start cutting to what they assume?
- **Timing.** Do they work at a pace that would survive a full column on a Saturday?
- **Finish.** Is the result something you would put in front of your own clients?
- **How they take direction.** If you or another stylist offers a suggestion mid-service, do they take it, or dig in?
- **How the room reacts to them.** Your other stylists will tell you afterwards, unprompted, whether they'd want this person on the next chair. That reaction is worth more than most interview scoring sheets.

An interview can be rehearsed. A trade test cannot. Someone can talk beautifully about client care and still turn a consultation into a monologue the moment there is a client in the chair.

## Structuring the first phone call

The first phone call has one job: decide fast whether it is worth bringing someone in for a trade test. Keep it short and cover three things, in this order.

1. **Can they actually start.** Notice period, days and hours they can work, employed or self-employed or chair-rental, and whether that matches what you are offering. This is the fastest possible filter, and it is astonishing how often it gets asked last, after a long chat about technique.
2. **What they actually do.** Not "what services do you offer" — what do they specialise in, what does a typical week look like, how would they describe their own client base. Listen for specifics. Vague answers here tend to mean a vague stylist.
3. **Why this salon.** Why they applied here, not just anywhere with a chair going. Someone who mentions something specific about your salon — the client base, the location, something a friend told them — is a different prospect from someone working through a long list of other adverts open in other tabs.

If all three land, book the trade test on that call, there and then, before you hang up. Every day between "that went well" and "come in Thursday" is a day a stronger salon can get to them first.

## Why speed of reply matters more than almost anything else

Speed of first reply matters because a stylist looking for a chair is very rarely looking at only one salon.

They apply to several places in the same week. The salon that replies first gets first go at a trade test, and the trade test is usually where the decision actually gets made. A salon that takes too long to reply is not competing on who has the better offer — they are competing on who never got the chance to make one, because the candidate had already trialled and accepted somewhere else.

This is why the "read them all on Sunday night" pattern is so costly. It is not that Sunday-night reading produces worse judgement. It is that the good candidates are gone by Sunday night, and the ones still waiting by then are disproportionately the ones nobody else wanted quickly either.

The fix does not require reading every CV the moment it lands. It requires replying the moment it lands — even a short message confirming you have it and naming a day you will call. That single message is often the difference between a candidate who stays warm and one who assumes the job is filled and moves on.

## What this looks like without a spreadsheet on the side

Hiring usually falls apart in the gap between three separate places: applications sitting in an inbox, a shortlist scribbled on a phone note, and a rota that has nothing to do with either. The candidate everyone liked at the trade test gets lost between the note and the rota, and the reply that should have gone out immediately goes out a week late instead, because whoever owns the inbox was on the floor all week.

The point of keeping applicants, trade tests and the rota in one place is not neatness for its own sake. It is that a starter who trialled well should move onto the rota the same day, not get typed into it from memory a week later once someone remembers. From advert to first day on the floor, one record, so nothing sits waiting on a Sunday that could have moved on a Tuesday.

## Start with the reply, not the read

If you take one thing from this: stop trying to read every CV properly before you reply to any of them. Reply first, read second.

A same-day acknowledgement, a short call within the week structured around start date, actual work, and why-this-salon, then a trade test for anyone who clears that bar. That order gets you to the same decision you would have reached after a week of careful reading — except you reach it while the good candidates are still available to hear it.

---

## Why is salon stock always going missing? Back bar control that works
Source: https://salonforge.com/blog/salon-stock-going-missing/
Published: 2026-07-24  ·  Updated: 2026-07-24

## Back bar and retail are two different problems

Back bar stock and retail stock go missing for different reasons, and counting them together in one stock take is why most salons can never explain the gap. Back bar is product used on the client during a service — colour, shampoo, conditioner, the treatment ampoule opened for a top-up, the tub of mask scooped out during a blow-dry. Retail is product sold to a client to take home — the same brand of shampoo, but bought at the till on the way out the door.

They drift for different reasons too. Back bar use should be tied to an appointment: a stylist opens a tube, some of it goes on a head, and unless that gets written down against the client record, it simply disappears from the count with no trace of why. Retail use should be tied to a sale rung at the till — if it isn't rung, or rung against the wrong product, the retail number drifts for reasons that have nothing to do with what's happening at the colour bowl.

Run one stock take covering both once a year and you get a single, frightening total with no way to split it — no way to tell whether it's colour going on more heads than the diary shows, retail walking out unpaid, or a supplier short-delivering a box that was never checked at the door. A combined number can't tell you, and a combined number is usually where "somebody must be stealing" starts.

| | Back bar | Retail |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | Product used on the client during the service | Product sold to the client to take home |
| Where it should be recorded | Against the appointment or colour formula | At the till, as a sale |
| Typical cause of a gap | Unlogged use — product used but never written down | Under-ringing, wrong item rung, unrecorded staff purchases |
| Who records it | The stylist, mid-service | The front desk, at the point of payment |
| What actually fixes it | Deducting automatically from what's weighed or used | Reconciling till sales against a physical count, regularly |

## Why "missing" stock almost never means theft

Most stock that looks missing was used, not stolen — it just never got written down. Picture an ordinary Saturday: a colour tube runs out partway through a long-haired client's foils, and a stylist grabs another off the shelf without stopping to log it because there's a queue at reception and a blow-dry waiting. A conditioner sachet goes home with a client after a complaint about dry ends, as a goodwill gesture nobody thought to record anywhere. A junior borrows a tester of the new range to try on her own hair over the weekend. A rep leaves samples that get handed out over a fortnight, uncounted in and uncounted out.

None of that is theft. All of it is product leaving the shelf without a matching entry anywhere, which is exactly what a stock take measures — the gap between what was bought and what's left, with no visibility into why.

> A number with no story attached always gets read as theft. Give it a story and it almost always isn't.

That doesn't mean theft never happens, in any salon, anywhere. It means it should be the last explanation reached for, not the first — and it should never be the explanation offered to a team before the unrecorded-use possibility has been ruled out. A team that feels accused over a number nobody can explain stops trusting whoever's doing the counting, which makes the real problem — the unrecorded use — harder to fix, not easier.

## Why an annual stock take tells you nothing useful

An annual count only proves that a gap exists — it can't tell you when it opened up, who was on the floor at the time, or which of the many small unlogged actions over the year added up to the total. By the time the count happens, the Tuesday afternoon that caused any particular loss is long gone from everyone's memory, and there's no way back to it.

Averages hide problems too. One colour line might be significantly over-used against what the diary says was booked, while a slower-moving retail line sits close to correct — net them together across a full range and the total can look almost fine while one shelf is badly wrong underneath it.

## What counting rhythm actually works

Counting little and often, tied to delivery and to the diary, beats one long reconciliation because it shrinks the time between a product disappearing and someone noticing.

- Check stock in against the delivery note as it arrives, before it goes on the shelf, not weeks later.
- Count the high-value back bar lines — colour, bond builders — weekly, against what the diary says was actually used that week.
- Reconcile retail against till sales weekly rather than monthly, while the week is still fresh enough that a mismatch means something.

None of this needs to be a large exercise. A five-minute count against a clear number, every week, catches drift while it's still small enough to explain.

## What changes when stock is deducted at the point of use

The picture changes completely once product is deducted the moment it's used, rather than estimated afterwards from a shelf count. Colour weighed on a connected scale and costed to the gram, written straight to the client record, means the formula a stylist actually mixed is the number that comes off the shelf — not an estimate, not a guess reconstructed at the end of the month. That's been recorded 19,949 times so far across six working salons, from London to Saudi Arabia, and in every one of those the amount used and the amount logged are the same figure, because they're the same act.

The same logic works away from the colour bowl. A drink poured for a client and logged against their name deducts from stock the moment it happens, so a round of coffees on a Friday afternoon is a recorded event tied to an appointment, not a mystery when someone totals the fridge in December.

Once use is recorded at the moment it happens, there's very little left to reconcile. Stock levels already reflect what actually happened on the floor, because every gram of colour and every drink logged came off the count the moment it was used, not weeks later at a stock take. And the conversation with the team changes shape entirely — from "the numbers don't add up, does anyone know why" to nothing at all, because there was never a gap left for anyone to explain.

---

## 12 questions to ask before switching salon software
Source: https://salonforge.com/blog/questions-before-switching-salon-software/
Published: 2026-07-24  ·  Updated: 2026-07-24

A salon changes its booking software about as often as it repaints the front desk — rarely, and usually because something broke rather than because the timing was right. That makes it hard to know what a normal changeover looks like, or which questions actually matter versus which ones a sales conversation is designed to steer you around.

These are the twelve worth asking. Ask them of us and ask them of anyone else on your shortlist. The honest answer to several of them is "it depends" — what matters is whether the person answering can tell you what it depends on.

## The shortlist

| Ask about | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Data ownership | Decides whether you can ever leave |
| The changeover | Decides how bad your worst Saturday gets |
| Per-stylist pricing | Decides what growth actually costs you |
| The exit | Decides what happens if this goes wrong |

## Your data

### 1. Who owns your client and appointment data — and can you export it yourself, any time you like?

The honest answer should be: you do, and you can pull it yourself without asking anyone's permission or waiting on a request. Try this before you sign, not after. Ask for a sample export of your current client list and appointment history, today, while you are still just looking. If the answer involves a support ticket, a delay, or a fee to get your own client list back, that is worth knowing now.

### 2. What happens to your appointment history — the bookings, the notes, the colour formulas, going back years?

This depends on what you ask for and what the provider migrates by default. Some systems bring years of history across as data you can still use — a stylist can open a client's record and see the actual colour formula from years back. Others only move a current client list, and the history becomes a static file you can look at but nothing on the new system can read. Ask for the date range in writing.

### 3. Will the export come out in a format another system can actually read?

There is a real difference between a plain file — the kind any other software can open and use — and a PDF or printout that just sits there. Ask to see an actual export, not a description of one. This is the question that protects you against whoever you switch to next, not just the one you are switching to now.

> The honest answer to most of these questions is "it depends" — the provider willing to say what it depends on is telling you more than the one with a rehearsed yes.

## The changeover

### 4. How long does the changeover really take, start to finish?

It depends on your salon's size, how many years of history you are bringing across, and how many stylists need their own price lists set up. Get real dates in writing rather than a verbal "a few days". Ask what "live" actually means too — a client list moved across is not the same as a rota built, prices set per stylist, and online booking switched over.

### 5. What happens on the first Saturday?

This is the question that separates a provider who has done this before from one reciting a pitch. Ask directly: if the online booking page breaks, or the front desk cannot find a client's history on a Saturday morning, who do you call, and are they actually answering calls that day. A provider who has not thought hard about the first Saturday has not run many changeovers.

### 6. Who trains your staff, and what happens to the stylist who is on holiday that week?

Ask whether training happens in person or over a call, once or on an ongoing basis, and what happens for the self-employed stylist who only works part of the week and misses the session entirely. A one-off training day works for a salon that is fully staffed and available. Most salons are not.

## The money

### 7. What does it cost when you add a stylist — or lose one?

Get the exact number per seat, not a banded price that turns out to depend on your total headcount.
